image-sensor-001.question: Which correctly describes the difference in how CCD and CMOS image sensors read out signals?
choices: A CCD converts charge to voltage with an amplifier in each pixel and reads it out row by row, while a CMOS sensor transfers charge like a bucket brigade to a single output amplifier
Neither converts light to charge; both read the light intensity directly as a change in resistance in each pixel and differ only in how the pixels are arranged
A CCD transfers charge pixel to pixel to a few output amplifiers that convert it to voltage, while a CMOS sensor converts it with an amplifier in each pixel and reads rows out
image-sensor-001.explanation: In both sensors a photodiode converts photons to electrons that are stored in the pixel. A CCD switches electrode voltages in sequence to transfer the charge to the neighboring pixel, and finally a few output amplifiers convert it to voltage. Transfer losses are very small and pixel-to-pixel variation is low, but transfer requires high voltages and large power. A CMOS image sensor is an active-pixel type with an amplifying transistor (source follower) in every pixel; rows are selected and read in parallel by per-column circuits, and everything up to AD conversion can be built on the same chip, making it fast and low in power. The choice that swaps the two is wrong. Reading light intensity as a change in resistance is what a photoconductive cell does, not the method of today's image sensors.

image-sensor-002.question: A pixel with a quantum efficiency of 60% receives an average of 10000 photons during the exposure. Considering only photon shot noise, which is closest to the S/N (signal electrons / noise electrons) of this pixel?
choices: About 77
About 100
About 60
image-sensor-002.explanation: The pixel collects on average 10000 × 0.6 = 6000 electrons. Photon arrivals are random and follow a Poisson distribution, and the electron count thinned by the quantum efficiency is also Poisson, so the noise (standard deviation) is the square root of the electron count, √6000 ≈ 77.5. The S/N is 6000/77.5 = √6000 ≈ 77, about 38 dB. About 100 is the square root of the 10000 incident photons, forgetting the quantum efficiency. About 60 divides the 6000-electron signal by 100, the square root of the photon count, mixing electrons and photons. The shot-noise-limited S/N is the square root of the number of collected electrons, so doubling the S/N needs four times the light. A device with a higher quantum efficiency gives better S/N for the same light.

image-sensor-003.question: Which is closest to the dynamic range of an image sensor with a full-well capacity (maximum number of electrons a pixel can hold) of 20000 and a read noise of 4 electrons (rms)? Express the dynamic range as the ratio of full-well capacity to read noise in 20 log₁₀.
choices: About 37 dB
About 74 dB
About 86 dB
image-sensor-003.explanation: Dynamic range is the ratio of the brightest to the darkest signal that one image can handle at once; the bright end is set by the full-well capacity and the dark end by the noise with no light (here the read noise). The ratio is 20000/4 = 5000, and 20 log₁₀ 5000 ≈ 74 dB. About 37 dB converts the electron ratio with 10 log₁₀ as if it were a power ratio; in image sensors the signal electron count is treated as an amplitude-like quantity, like voltage, and 20 log₁₀ is the usual choice. About 86 dB takes the ratio 20000 as if the read noise were 1 electron. Note that the S/N near full well is only √20000 ≈ 141 (about 43 dB); dynamic range and S/N are different quantities.

image-sensor-004.question: In a dark scene a pixel's signal is on average 16 electrons and the read noise is 3 electrons (rms). Dark current is negligible and the only noise sources are the signal's shot noise and the read noise. Which is closest to the S/N?
choices: About 4.0
About 3.2
About 5.3
image-sensor-004.explanation: Independent noise sources add in variance (in squares). The shot-noise variance equals the signal electron count, 16, and the read-noise variance is 3² = 9, so the total noise is √(16 + 9) = 5 electrons. The S/N is 16/5 = 3.2. About 4.0 is √16 = 4 from shot noise alone and overlooks the read noise. About 5.3 is 16/3 with read noise alone. Where the signal is below the square of the read noise (here 9 electrons), read noise dominates; above it, shot noise dominates. This is why low-noise sensors with 1 to 2 electrons of read noise have the advantage in dark scenes, while in bright scenes every sensor's S/N is set by the photon shot noise.

image-sensor-005.question: In a CMOS image sensor pixel, the floating diffusion that converts charge to voltage has a capacitance of 2 fF. Which correctly pairs the voltage per electron (conversion gain) with the effect of making this capacitance smaller? (q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)
choices: About 80 µV per electron. A smaller capacitance gives more voltage per electron and improves both the read noise and the full-well capacity
About 8 µV per electron. A smaller capacitance gives more voltage per electron, lowering the read noise referred to electrons, but reduces the full-well capacity
About 80 µV per electron. A smaller capacitance gives more voltage per electron, lowering the read noise referred to electrons, but reduces the full-well capacity
image-sensor-005.explanation: Putting charge Q on capacitance C gives V = Q/C, so one electron gives q/C = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹/(2×10⁻¹⁵) = 8×10⁻⁵ V, about 80 µV. A smaller capacitance raises the conversion gain, so the noise (voltage) of later circuits referred to electrons becomes smaller, which helps in dark scenes. On the other hand, the range over which the floating-diffusion voltage can swing is set by the supply voltage and so on; with a 1 V swing, for example, 2 fF handles about 12500 electrons and 1 fF about 6250, so the bright end of the dynamic range narrows. The choice where both improve overlooks this trade-off. About 8 µV comes from converting fF incorrectly as 10⁻¹⁴ F.

image-sensor-006.question: Which correctly describes the role of correlated double sampling (CDS) used in CMOS image sensors?
choices: It takes the difference between the voltage just after reset and the voltage after charge transfer, cancelling the kTC noise that varies at every reset and the amplifier offset
It exposes the same pixel twice in a row and adds the results, doubling the signal while the random photon shot noise, which flips sign between the two, cancels out
It takes the difference between the signals of two neighboring pixels to enhance the subject's edges and make the in-focus position easier to detect
image-sensor-006.explanation: When the floating diffusion is reset, the voltage on its capacitance C retains a thermal-noise spread of √(kT/C) (kTC noise), and its value changes at every reset. In CDS, the voltage after reset (reset level) is read first, then the voltage after the photodiode's charge is transferred (signal level), and their difference is taken as the signal. Both readings contain the same reset noise and amplifier offset, so the difference cancels them and also reduces fixed-pattern variation between pixels. Photon shot noise is a fluctuation of the light itself, so no circuit can cancel it, and adding two exposures improves the S/N only as the square root of the light. Differencing neighboring pixels is edge enhancement, a separate image-processing step from CDS.

image-sensor-007.question: In a cooled camera, the image sensor's temperature is lowered by 21 K. If the dark current halves for every 7 K of cooling, which correctly pairs the change in dark current with the change in the dark-current shot noise (same exposure time)?
choices: Dark current about 1/8, and dark-current shot noise also about 1/8
Dark current about 1/3, dark-current shot noise about 1/1.7
Dark current about 1/8, dark-current shot noise about 1/2.8
image-sensor-007.explanation: Dark current is the current of thermally excited electrons that accumulate independently of light, and it changes exponentially with temperature. If it halves every 7 K, cooling by 21 K gives 2³ = 8, so the dark current falls to about 1/8. The electrons collected from dark current also follow a Poisson distribution, so their noise is proportional to the square root of the electron count, and √8 ≈ 2.8 gives about 1/2.8. The choice with noise also at 1/8 assumes the noise is proportional to the electron count. The choice with about 1/3 mistakes 21/7 = 3 for the factor, treating the exponential change as if it were proportional. The temperature step that halves the dark current varies by device from a few K to about 10 K, so the 7 K here is a rule-of-thumb value. Cooling is used for long exposures such as astronomical imaging.

image-sensor-008.question: Which correctly describes the Bayer color filter array widely used in color image sensors?
choices: Red, green and blue filters are arranged in equal numbers in a checkerboard and each pixel measures all three colors, so no color interpolation from neighboring pixels is needed
In each 2×2 block two pixels are green and one each red and blue, sampling more of the green the eye is most sensitive to; missing colors are interpolated from neighbors
Two of every 2×2 pixels are green because silicon's quantum efficiency is lowest at green wavelengths, and the combined signal of two pixels makes up for the shortfall in sensitivity
image-sensor-008.explanation: The Bayer array places green in a checkerboard and red and blue in the remaining positions on alternate rows, so half the pixels are green and a quarter each are red and blue. The human luminous efficiency is high in the green, and green carries much of the image's brightness (luminance) information, so sampling more green favors resolving fine light-and-dark detail. Each pixel measures only the one color passed by its filter, so the values of the other two colors are found by demosaicing, interpolation from surrounding pixels, and false color can appear in fine patterns. Red and blue are sampled only once every two pixels in each direction, so color resolution is lower than luminance resolution. Measuring three colors per pixel is done by three-sensor systems or special schemes that separate colors by depth. In the visible, silicon's quantum efficiency is low rather on the blue side, so compensating for green sensitivity is not the reason.

image-sensor-009.question: What is the main reason an infrared-cut filter is placed in front of a digital camera's image sensor?
choices: Silicon is sensitive in the near infrared up to about 1.1 µm and color filters pass near infrared, so invisible infrared light causes errors in color and brightness
Infrared absorption damages the silicon crystal and increases pixel defects, so the filter protects the device during long exposures
Infrared light is not absorbed in silicon and passes through the device, so the filter prevents light reflected from the package behind it from causing ghosts and flare
image-sensor-009.explanation: Silicon's band gap is about 1.12 eV, so light shorter than about 1.1 µm is absorbed and produces electrons, and the sensitivity is considerable in the near infrared around 700 to 1000 nm. The organic-dye red, green and blue filters of a Bayer array pass some near-infrared light, so without removing it, color reproduction departs from human vision; for example, fabric that looks black to the eye is recorded with a reddish-purple tint. A filter passing only visible light is therefore used to bring the response closer to the eye's. The device is not damaged by infrared light, and surveillance cameras remove the filter to shoot at night under near-infrared illumination. Infrared passes through silicon only at wavelengths longer than about 1.1 µm; light at 700 to 1000 nm is absorbed and becomes signal.

image-sensor-010.question: For a CMOS image sensor with small pixels, what is the main reason a backside-illuminated (BSI) structure has an advantage over a front-illuminated one?
choices: Illuminating from the back allows a thicker silicon layer, so even near-infrared light with a long absorption length is well absorbed and the near-infrared quantum efficiency rises greatly
Light enters the photodiode from the side opposite the wiring, so it is not blocked or scattered by metal wiring and oblique light is also collected well
Illuminating from the back keeps heat generated in the wiring from reaching the photodiode through the substrate, lowering its temperature so that dark current almost disappears
image-sensor-010.explanation: In a front-illuminated sensor, several layers of metal wiring sit above the photodiode, and light reaches it through gaps in the wiring. As pixels shrink, the wiring occupies a larger share, part of the light is blocked even with microlenses, and obliquely incident light scatters into neighboring pixels and causes color crosstalk. A backside-illuminated sensor thins the wafer and lets light in from the back, where there is no wiring, so nothing obstructs the light-receiving surface, the aperture fraction and angular response improve, and small pixels keep their sensitivity. Backside illumination actually thins the silicon to a few µm, so near-infrared light with its long absorption length passes through more easily. The illumination direction does not lower the temperature, and treatment is needed to suppress dark current from defects at the thinned surface.

image-sensor-011.question: Compare two ways of binning, treating the signals of a 2×2 block of four pixels as one pixel: adding the charges and reading out once, as in a CCD, and reading each of the four pixels in a CMOS image sensor and adding them digitally. Which correctly describes the S/N in a dark scene?
choices: Both give four times the signal, and the only noise change is a fourfold shot-noise variance in each, so even in a dark scene the S/N is exactly the same
In digital addition the read noise averages away over the four readouts, so in a dark scene digital addition gives the better S/N
Both give four times the signal, but charge addition adds the read noise once while digital addition adds it four times in variance, so in a dark scene charge addition gives the better S/N
image-sensor-011.explanation: Either way the number of collected electrons is four times larger, and the photon shot-noise variance is also four times larger. The difference is the read noise: reading once after adding charge leaves a read-noise variance of σr², but reading four pixels separately and adding gives 4σr², doubling the noise. For example, with 25 electrons per pixel and σr = 4 electrons, charge addition gives 100/√(100 + 16) ≈ 9.3 and digital addition gives 100/√(100 + 64) ≈ 7.8. In bright scenes shot noise dominates and the difference is small, but in dark scenes charge addition has the advantage. The choice with the same S/N overlooks the difference in the number of readouts. Adding independent noise increases it in variance; it never averages away.

image-sensor-012.question: When a fast, horizontally moving subject is shot with the rolling shutter of a CMOS image sensor, which correctly pairs the phenomenon that tends to occur with its reason?
choices: The image is distorted, e.g. vertical poles appear slanted, because each row's exposure starts slightly later, so the subject is recorded at different positions in upper and lower rows
The whole image is blurred uniformly, because with a rolling shutter all pixels are exposed simultaneously for longer than with a global shutter
No distortion occurs, because even if the exposure times differ by row, all rows are read out together at the end and recorded at the same time
image-sensor-012.explanation: A rolling shutter resets and reads out row by row in sequence, so although every row has the same exposure duration, its start and end times shift slightly from top to bottom. If reading one frame takes, say, several tens of ms, a subject moving sideways in that time is recorded at different positions in upper and lower rows, so vertical poles slant and spinning propellers appear bent. Under rapidly flickering lighting, bands of light and dark can also appear row by row. Exposing all pixels simultaneously is the global-shutter scheme, which needs a storage element in each pixel to hold the charge temporarily. Uniform blur of the whole image is motion blur from a long exposure and is not specific to rolling shutters. Grouping the readout order does not remove the shift in exposure timing.

image-sensor-013.question: An aberration-free lens stopped down to f/8 images a point source with 550 nm light. Which is closest to the diameter of the first dark ring of the diffraction point image (Airy disk)?
choices: About 10.7 µm
About 5.4 µm
About 4.4 µm
image-sensor-013.explanation: For an aberration-free lens with a circular aperture, the radius of the first dark ring of the point image is 1.22λN and its diameter is 2.44λN (N is the f-number). With λ = 0.55 µm and N = 8, this gives 2.44 × 0.55 × 8 ≈ 10.7 µm. On a sensor with a 4 µm pixel pitch the point image spreads over about 2.7 pixels, so on small sensors with fine pixels, too large an f-number makes the diffraction blur larger than a pixel and fine detail actually softens (diffraction softening). About 5.4 µm mistakes the radius 1.22λN for the diameter. About 4.4 µm computes only λN and drops the coefficient. Even when you want a deeper depth of field, a rule of thumb is to choose an aperture where the diffraction blur stays inconspicuous compared with the pixel size.

image-sensor-014.question: A photo is taken with a 50 mm f/2 lens on a 35 mm full-frame sensor. With the same angle of view and the same subject distance, it is taken again with a sensor of half the diagonal and a 25 mm f/2 lens. When both are enlarged to the same viewing size, which correctly describes the depth of field? Assume the subject distance is much shorter than the hyperfocal distance and that the depth of field is about 2Ncs²/f² (N is the f-number, c the permissible circle of confusion, s the subject distance, f the focal length).
choices: The f-number is the same f/2, so the image-plane brightness is the same and so is the depth of field as with 35 mm full frame
A smaller sensor has a proportionally smaller circle of confusion, so at the same f-number the depth of field becomes shallower
The depth of field is about twice as deep, about the same as stopping the 35 mm full-frame camera down to f/4
image-sensor-014.explanation: To enlarge to the same size, the small sensor's image is magnified twice as much, so the circle of confusion c must also be halved. In 2Ncs²/f², c is 1/2 and f is 1/2, so the depth of field becomes (1/2)/(1/2)² = 2 times deeper. Matching it on 35 mm full frame requires doubling N to f/4, the idea known as the equivalent f-number. The choice that the same f-number gives the same depth of field confuses image-plane brightness (set by the f-number) with depth of field. The smaller circle of confusion does have an effect, but the shorter focal length acts as its square, so overall the depth becomes deeper. This is why backgrounds are hard to blur with small-sensor smartphones.

image-sensor-015.question: Which correctly describes raising the ISO setting of a digital camera (raising the analog gain on the sensor output)?
choices: Raising the ISO setting raises the photodiode bias and its quantum efficiency, so more electrons are collected from the same light and the S/N in dark scenes fundamentally improves
Photon numbers do not increase, so the S/N set by shot noise is unchanged. Later-stage noise matters relatively less, but saturation comes sooner and the dynamic range narrows
Raising the ISO setting increases the full-well capacity, so bright areas saturate less easily and, together with the dark areas, the dynamic range widens
image-sensor-015.explanation: The ISO setting decides by how much the signal, after conversion to electrons in the pixel, is amplified before recording; it does not change the quantum efficiency that converts photons to electrons or the full-well capacity the pixel can hold. The number of electrons collected in a dark scene is set by the exposure time, the f-number and the subject's brightness, and so is the S/N set by photon shot noise. Raising the gain makes the noise added after the amplifier and in AD conversion smaller when referred to electrons, so it does reduce shadow noise somewhat. However, the number of electrons that reaches the AD converter's maximum falls in inverse proportion to the gain, so highlights saturate more easily and the dynamic range narrows. The choices in which quantum efficiency or full-well capacity changes confuse gain with properties of the pixel.

image-sensor-016.question: When an interline-transfer CCD image sensor photographs a scene containing a strong light source such as the sun or a lamp, a bright vertical line sometimes appears above and below the source. Which is the main cause of this phenomenon (smear)?
choices: Multiple reflections of the strong light inside the lens produce rings and spots around the source, which are stretched along the sensor's readout direction and appear as a vertical line
The intense light locally heats the photodiode, increasing the dark current of every pixel in the same column together so that only that column becomes brighter as a vertical line
Some of the intense light leaks into the vertical transfer channels, and charge generated deep in the silicon diffuses into them, adding to the charge being transferred
image-sensor-016.explanation: In an interline CCD, each column of photodiodes has a light-shielded vertical transfer channel beside it that carries charge downward for readout. Under intense light, some light leaks through gaps in the shield into the channel, and charge generated deep in the silicon diffuses in as well. All the charge packets being transferred through that column pick up this extra charge, producing a bright vertical line above and below the source. A CMOS image sensor converts charge to voltage with an amplifier in each pixel and does not move charge along the columns, so this kind of smear does not occur. Multiple reflections in the lens cause flare and ghosts, not vertical lines, and local heating does not raise the dark current of a whole column uniformly.

image-sensor-017.question: An image sensor records a uniformly illuminated image. After subtracting the dark image, the mean signal is 2000 DN and the temporal variance of each pixel is 1000 DN². If read noise is negligible and the fluctuations are due only to photon shot noise, which value is closest to the conversion gain (electrons per DN)? DN is the output unit of the A/D converter.
choices: About 0.5 e⁻/DN
About 2.0 e⁻/DN
About 45 e⁻/DN
image-sensor-017.explanation: With a conversion gain K [e⁻/DN], the number of electrons is N = 2000K, and its shot-noise variance is N (in electrons squared). In DN the variance is N/K² = 2000/K, so 2000/K = 1000 gives K = 2.0 e⁻/DN and a signal of about 4000 electrons. About 0.5 e⁻/DN is the variance divided by the mean, which inverts the relation between DN and electrons. About 45 e⁻/DN is simply the square root of the mean, √2000. Plotting variance against mean for many illumination levels (the photon transfer curve) gives the conversion gain from the slope 1/K and the read noise from the dark end.

image-sensor-018.question: An image sensor has a pixel-to-pixel sensitivity variation (PRNU) of 1%. When it images a bright, uniform surface that accumulates an average of 40000 electrons, which statement about this variation is correct?
choices: The variation scales with the signal, amounting to about 400 electrons, larger than the shot noise (about 200), but it can be removed by flat-field correction, dividing by an image of a uniform surface
The variation is constant regardless of signal, so it becomes relatively smaller at higher brightness, is negligible compared with the shot noise (about 200), and needs no correction
The variation is noise that changes randomly with time, so taking and averaging many images of the same scene reduces it, but it cannot be corrected by dividing by an image of a uniform surface
image-sensor-018.explanation: PRNU is the difference in sensitivity between pixels, a fixed-pattern noise proportional to the signal. At 1% it amounts to about 400 electrons out of 40000, twice the shot noise √40000 = 200. Without correction the S/N falls from 200, set by shot noise alone, to 40000/√(200² + 400²) ≈ 89. Because each pixel always has the same deviation, dividing by an image of a uniform surface (a flat-field image) removes it. A constant variation independent of signal describes the fixed pattern of dark current and offsets (DSNU), which matters in dark scenes. PRNU does not change with time, so averaging many frames does not reduce it.

image-sensor-019.question: In optics such as smartphone cameras, where the lens is thin and close to the sensor, the chief ray arrives more obliquely toward the edge of the image (a larger chief ray angle). Which combination of effect and countermeasure is correct?
choices: At peripheral pixels, more oblique light travels a longer path in the silicon and is absorbed more, so the edges appear brighter than the center, which image processing darkens to match
The chief ray angle does not affect image brightness, but it increases distortion, so pixels are spaced more widely toward the edge to cancel the distortion
At peripheral pixels the focused spot shifts off the photodiode, causing shading and color crosstalk, so the microlenses and color filters are shifted toward the center
image-sensor-019.explanation: The microlens over each pixel is designed to focus light arriving from directly above onto the photodiode. Light arriving obliquely shifts the focal spot sideways, so it is blocked by wiring or pixel boundaries or enters the neighboring pixel, causing shading (darkening toward the edge) and color crosstalk, as light through a neighboring color filter mixes in. The microlenses and color filters are therefore shifted gradually toward the center to match the chief ray angle at each position on the sensor. For oblique light, the loss from the shifted focus dominates, so the edges do not become brighter. Distortion is corrected by lens design or image processing, and the pixels remain evenly spaced.

image-sensor-020.question: A full-well capacity of 20000 electrons is mapped onto the full range (4096 steps) of a 12-bit A/D converter. Which value is closest to the quantization noise (an rms value of 1/√12 of one step) expressed in electrons?
choices: About 4.9 electrons
About 1.4 electrons
About 2.4 electrons
image-sensor-020.explanation: One step corresponds to 20000/4096 ≈ 4.9 electrons. The quantization error can be regarded as uniformly distributed between −0.5 and +0.5 step, with an rms value of 1/√12 ≈ 0.29 of a step, so 4.9 × 0.29 ≈ 1.4 electrons. About 4.9 electrons is one full step, and about 2.4 electrons is half a step; these confuse the maximum error with the rms value. With a read noise of, say, 3 electrons, the total noise rises slightly to √(3² + 1.4²) ≈ 3.3 electrons. For sensors with low read noise, the effect of quantization noise is reduced by using more bits or by applying high gain to dark signals before conversion.

image-sensor-021.question: To remove the pixel-to-pixel non-uniformity of dark current (fixed pattern) from a long-exposure image, a dark frame taken at the same temperature and exposure time is subtracted. Let the temporal noise of the light image be σ, and let each dark frame have independent noise of the same size σ. Which combination correctly gives the noise after subtracting a single dark frame and after subtracting the average of 16 dark frames?
choices: Single frame: still σ; average of 16: about 0.25σ
Single frame: about 2σ; average of 16: about 1.06σ
Single frame: about 1.41σ; average of 16: about 1.03σ
image-sensor-021.explanation: Independent noises add in variance. Subtracting one dark frame gives a variance of σ² + σ² = 2σ², so the noise grows to √2σ ≈ 1.41σ. The average of 16 dark frames has noise σ/√16 = σ/4, so after subtraction the noise is √(σ² + σ²/16) ≈ 1.03σ. The option keeping σ ignores the noise of the subtracted frame and wrongly lets averaging also reduce the noise of the light image. About 2σ adds the noise amplitudes instead of variances (σ + σ), and about 1.06σ also assumes averaging cuts the noise to 1/16 (σ + σ/16). Averaging many dark frames removes only the fixed pattern, so astrophotography and fluorescence imaging record many dark frames.

image-sensor-022.question: Many CMOS image sensor pixels use a pinned (buried) photodiode, with a heavily doped p⁺ layer over the surface side of the photodiode, and a transfer gate that moves the charge to the floating diffusion (the four-transistor pixel). Which is a correct advantage of this structure?
choices: The p⁺ layer suppresses dark current from surface states, and charge is transferred completely, so there is no image lag, and correlated double sampling also removes reset noise
The strong field in the p⁺ layer causes avalanche multiplication of electrons, so one photon yields many electrons and read noise referred to electrons becomes practically negligible
The photodiode capacitance itself serves as the floating-diffusion capacitance, so the conversion gain rises while the capacitance stays large, and the full-well capacity also increases
image-sensor-022.explanation: The silicon–oxide interface has many surface states, and where a depletion region touches it, electrons and holes are generated thermally as dark current. A surface p⁺ layer keeps the depletion region away from the interface and fills the surface states with holes, sharply lowering dark current. The potential profile is also fixed by design, so opening the transfer gate moves all the stored electrons to the floating diffusion, leaving no lag from the previous image. Because the reset level can be read before the charge is transferred, correlated double sampling removes the kTC noise. The p⁺ layer does not cause avalanche multiplication. The idea of this pixel is to separate charge storage from charge-to-voltage conversion, keeping the floating diffusion small for high conversion gain.

image-sensor-023.question: Which is a correct drawback that a global-shutter CMOS image sensor, which exposes all pixels at the same time, tends to have compared with a rolling-shutter sensor?
choices: All pixels are exposed and read out at once with parallel readout circuits, so read noise grows in proportion to the square root of the number of pixels
Each pixel needs a storage node to hold its charge, which tends to reduce the light-sensitive area and full-well capacity, and light leaking into the node and dark current cause errors
Exposure timing shifts from row to row, so fast-moving subjects are skewed, and flickering lighting produces horizontal bright and dark bands
image-sensor-023.explanation: A global shutter ends the exposure of all pixels at once and then reads the rows out in turn. Holding the charge (or voltage) in the meantime requires a storage node in each pixel, which tends to shrink the photodiode area and full-well capacity. Light leaking into the storage node while it waits adds spurious charge (parasitic light sensitivity), and dark current accumulates during the hold. Readout is still row by row, so read noise does not grow with the square root of the pixel count. Skew and banding from row-by-row exposure timing are features of the rolling shutter, which the global shutter is designed to avoid.

image-sensor-024.question: A CCD with a read noise of 50 e⁻ (rms) has an electron-multiplying stage before the readout amplifier that increases the signal electrons with a gain G = 500 (EMCCD). Which value is closest to the read noise referred to the number of signal electrons before multiplication?
choices: About 0.1 e⁻
About 2.2 e⁻
About 25000 e⁻
image-sensor-024.explanation: The multiplication stage comes before the readout amplifier, so the signal is multiplied by G but the read noise, added at the amplifier, is not. Referred to the input electrons it is 50/500 = 0.1 e⁻, so even a one-photon signal can be distinguished above the read noise. About 25000 e⁻ multiplies the noise by the gain, referring it in the wrong direction. About 2.2 e⁻ divides by the square root of the gain. The multiplication is random, however, giving an excess noise factor of about √2, so in bright, shot-noise-limited conditions the S/N is as poor as if the quantum efficiency were halved. EMCCDs win only in very dim conditions where read noise dominates.

image-sensor-025.question: Which correctly describes dual conversion gain, in which each pixel's signal is read both with a high conversion gain and with a low conversion gain and combined into one image?
choices: Reading twice counts the photons twice, so the shot-noise-limited S/N of bright areas improves by √2
Lowering the conversion gain reduces the number of electrons that can be handled, so dark areas are read with low conversion gain and bright areas with high conversion gain
Dark areas are read with high conversion gain to make the read noise in electrons small, bright areas with low conversion gain to handle many electrons, and combining them widens the dynamic range
image-sensor-025.explanation: A smaller floating-diffusion capacitance gives more voltage per electron (higher conversion gain) and lower read noise referred to electrons, but fewer electrons fit within the allowed voltage swing. Dual conversion gain switches the capacitance to read the same charge under both conditions, then combines the high-gain values for dark areas with the low-gain values for bright areas, extending both ends of the dynamic range. Because the same exposure's charge is read, moving subjects show less misregistration than with methods that merge images of different exposure times. Reading twice does not increase the photon count, so shot noise is unchanged. Using low gain for dark areas reverses the relation between gain and noise.

image-sensor-026.question: A scene is correctly exposed at f/2.8 and 1/500 s. To increase the depth of field it is shot at f/5.6 instead. Without changing the sensitivity setting, which shutter speed gives the same exposure? (Exposure is proportional to exposure time and inversely proportional to the square of the f-number.)
image-sensor-026.explanation: Image-plane illuminance is inversely proportional to the square of the f-number, so going from f/2.8 to f/5.6 gives (5.6/2.8)² = 4, and the light drops to a quarter (two stops). For the same exposure the time is multiplied by 4: 1/500 × 4 = 1/125 s. 1/250 s assumes the exposure is proportional to the f-number and doubles the time, leaving it one stop short. 1/1000 s shortens the time instead and is three stops short. The f-number series 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6 goes up by about √2 per step, halving the light each time. Longer exposures make subject and camera blur more likely, so with moving subjects this is traded off against raising the sensitivity setting.

image-sensor-027.question: Light at 550 nm falls uniformly with an irradiance of 1.0 µW/cm² on an image sensor with 3.0 µm × 3.0 µm pixels and a quantum efficiency of 60%. Which value is closest to the number of electrons collected in one pixel during a 10 ms exposure? (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 1.5×10³
About 2.5×10³
About 0.15
image-sensor-027.explanation: The pixel area is (3.0×10⁻⁴ cm)² = 9.0×10⁻⁸ cm², so the power on the pixel is 1.0×10⁻⁶ × 9.0×10⁻⁸ = 9.0×10⁻¹⁴ W, and the energy in 10 ms is 9.0×10⁻¹⁶ J. One photon carries hc/λ = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 3.0×10⁸/550×10⁻⁹ ≈ 3.6×10⁻¹⁹ J, so about 2.5×10³ photons arrive, and multiplying by the quantum efficiency gives about 1.5×10³ electrons. About 2.5×10³ forgets the quantum efficiency, and about 0.15 expresses the area in m² without converting the irradiance to W/m². With about 1.5×10³ electrons the shot noise is about 39 electrons, so the S/N is about 39.

image-sensor-028.question: When a CMOS image sensor photographs a dark, uniform scene, the image sometimes shows a series of thin vertical stripes. Which combination of main cause and correction is correct?
choices: Photon shot noise in individual pixels happens to line up vertically and appears at different places each time, so averaging many frames does not reduce the stripe pattern at all
Astigmatism in the lens smears only the vertical lines, so stopping down or shooting at the center of the frame removes the stripes without any correction on the sensor side
Offsets and gains differ among the readout amplifiers and A/D converters provided for each column, and the stripes are corrected by measuring and subtracting each column's offset
image-sensor-028.explanation: In a CMOS image sensor, the pixels in one column share that column's readout circuit (amplifier and A/D converter). Small differences in offset or gain between these circuits shift all the pixels of a column together, producing vertical stripes (column fixed-pattern noise). The eye is sensitive to line patterns, so the stripes are noticeable even when smaller than the pixel-to-pixel variation. Because the pattern is the same every time, it can be corrected by measuring each column's offset in optically black pixels or dark frames and subtracting it. Shot noise is random in time and does not keep lining up in columns. Aberrations only blur the optical image and cannot create vertical stripes in a dark, uniform image.

image-sensor-029.question: In a photo with a bright light source in the frame, the pixels around the image of the source also turned white and spread out (blooming). Which combination of mechanism and remedy is correct?
choices: Charge exceeding the full-well capacity of a pixel's photodiode overflows into neighboring pixels; it is suppressed by providing a drain path that removes the excess charge
Strong light raises the quantum efficiency of a pixel and even the sensitivity of its neighbors; this depends only on the source brightness, so shortening the exposure cannot suppress it
Light from the source heats the readout wiring and raises the dark current of the surrounding pixels, so cooling the sensor suppresses it
image-sensor-029.explanation: The number of electrons a photodiode can hold is limited by its full-well capacity, and charge exceeding that limit under strong light spills into neighboring pixels and elsewhere. As a result, the surrounding pixels gain charge even though no light falls on them, and the image spreads out in white. The remedy is a drain path (anti-blooming structure) that carries excess charge to the substrate or reset supply before it overflows. This is a different mechanism from smear, in which light leaks into the transfer channels of a CCD and makes a vertical line. Quantum efficiency does not rise with light intensity, and dark current cannot increase fast enough during an exposure to cause such spreading. Shortening the exposure or stopping down reduces the overflowing charge and shrinks the spread.

image-sensor-030.question: Compare a monochrome image sensor without a color filter array (Bayer pattern) to a color sensor with the same pixel structure. Which statement correctly describes the monochrome sensor when photographing a white subject?
choices: The amount of light reaching each pixel is the same without the filters, but since no color interpolation is needed, only the noise is halved
No filter absorbs most of the visible light, so each pixel gets about two to three times more light, and full resolution comes without interpolation
Without the filters, infrared light blurs the image, so the sensitivity is lower than the color sensor's and the resolution is also lower because there is no interpolation
image-sensor-030.explanation: A Bayer filter passes only the band of one color, red, green or blue, at each pixel, so it transmits only about a third of white light. A monochrome sensor without filters receives the whole visible band, so it collects about two to three times more electrons in the same exposure and achieves a better S/N. Each pixel also measures brightness directly, so no demosaicing from neighboring pixels is needed, there are no false colors, and the resolution matches the pixel count. Saying the light per pixel is the same overlooks the absorption in the filters. When infrared must be removed, a separate filter is used. In fluorescence microscopy and astronomy, colors are sometimes captured one at a time with a monochrome sensor by changing filters.

image-sensor-031.question: A lens of 24 mm focal length is mounted on a 36 mm × 24 mm sensor to photograph a distant landscape. For a distortion-free lens, which value is closest to the horizontal angle of view (the full angle captured)?
choices: About 37°
About 56°
About 74°
image-sensor-031.explanation: The horizontal angle of view is 2 arctan(w/(2f)) = 2 arctan(18/24) = 2 × 36.9° ≈ 73.7°, about 74°. A distant object is imaged one focal length behind the lens, and the angle that fits within half the sensor width, 18 mm, is the half-angle. About 37° mistakes the half-angle arctan(18/24) for the full angle. About 56° takes arctan(36/24), turning the full sensor width divided by the focal length directly into an angle. With the same lens, a smaller sensor gives a narrower angle of view, and matching the angle requires a focal length proportional to the sensor size. The angle of view depends on focal length and sensor size, not on the f-number.

image-sensor-032.question: An uncooled camera takes a 20 s exposure. The mean signal is 400 electrons per pixel, the dark current is 5 e⁻/s per pixel, and the read noise is 10 e⁻ rms. Assuming the mean dark signal is removed by subtracting a dark frame, which value is closest to the S/N? (The only noise sources are shot noise of the signal and of the dark current, and read noise, all independent.)
choices: About 16
About 18
About 10
image-sensor-032.explanation: The dark current accumulates 5 × 20 = 100 electrons; its mean can be subtracted, but its shot noise of √100 = 10 electrons remains. Independent noises add in variance: √(400 + 100 + 10²) = √600 ≈ 24.5 electrons. The S/N is 400/24.5 ≈ 16.3, about 16. About 18 forgets the dark-current shot noise and divides by √(400 + 10²). About 10 adds the three noise amplitudes (20 + 10 + 10) directly; independent noises combine as the square root of the sum of squares. Dark-current noise matters in long exposures, so sensors are cooled to reduce the dark current.

image-sensor-033.question: Small CMOS image sensors with pixels around 1 µm often have deep trenches etched into the silicon between neighboring photodiodes and filled with an insulator (deep trench isolation, DTI). Which is its main purpose?
choices: The trenches increase the photodiode volume and hence the full-well capacity, preserving the dynamic range of small pixels even as they shrink
They keep obliquely incident light and deeply generated charge from reaching neighboring pixels, reducing color mixing and loss of resolution
Light travels along the trenches like a waveguide and separates by wavelength, so the colors can be separated without using any color filters at all
image-sensor-033.explanation: As pixels shrink, obliquely incident light can travel inside the silicon into the region of a neighboring pixel, and charge generated deep in the silicon by long-wavelength light can diffuse and be collected by the neighboring photodiode. This optical and electrical crosstalk mixes colors, lowers saturation, and reduces resolution. DTI builds walls of low-index insulator between pixels that reflect the light and block charge motion, suppressing the crosstalk. The trenches actually take area away from the pixel, so increasing the full-well capacity is not their purpose. They do not split light by wavelength either; color is separated by the color filters.

image-sensor-034.question: In a region with 50 Hz mains, a CMOS image sensor with a rolling shutter records video at a 1/1000 s exposure under lighting driven by AC (its brightness varies 100 times per second), and horizontal light and dark bands may appear across the frame. Which combination correctly gives the cause and the remedy?
choices: Rows are exposed at slightly different times and so at different phases of the flicker; setting the exposure to an integer multiple of 1/100 s removes the bands
Ultraviolet light in the illumination interferes in the films on the sensor surface; fitting a UV-blocking filter in front of the lens removes the bands
The flicker changes the sensor temperature so the dark current differs row by row; cooling the sensor to reduce dark current removes the bands
image-sensor-034.explanation: A rolling shutter exposes the rows from top to bottom with slightly staggered start times. When the brightness varies with a period of 1/100 s and the exposure is short, different rows are exposed during bright and dark phases, which appears as horizontal bands. Setting the exposure to an integer multiple of the 1/100 s period (1/100 s, 1/50 s, and so on) gives every row a whole number of periods of light, equalizing the rows and removing the bands. In 60 Hz regions the exposure is set to multiples of 1/120 s. Ultraviolet interference and flicker-induced changes in dark current are not the cause. With a global shutter, which exposes all pixels at once, the flicker appears as frame-to-frame brightness variation rather than bands.

image-sensor-035.question: In a silicon photodiode, the depth at which light is absorbed varies greatly with wavelength. Which combination correctly describes how the absorption depth varies across the visible and near infrared and what follows from it?
choices: Red light is absorbed closest to the surface, so it suffers most from recombination at surface defects, and of the three colors red quantum efficiency drops the most
The absorption depth is nearly the same for all wavelengths, and the wavelength dependence of quantum efficiency is set only by the color-filter transmittance
Blue light is absorbed within about 1 µm of the surface, while red and near-infrared light go several micrometers or more, so thin absorbing layers lose long-wavelength efficiency
image-sensor-035.explanation: The absorption coefficient of silicon is larger at shorter wavelengths; the depth at which the intensity falls to 1/e is about 0.4 µm at 450 nm, about 3 µm at 650 nm, and about 20 µm at 850 nm. Blue light is absorbed very near the surface and is sensitive to recombination at surface defects, while red and near-infrared light penetrate deeply, so pixels with an absorbing layer only a few micrometers thick let part of it pass through unabsorbed, lowering the quantum efficiency. Near-infrared sensors therefore use thick absorbing layers or structures that scatter light obliquely to lengthen its path. Absorbing red closest to the surface reverses the trend. The wavelength dependence of absorption depth is also the principle of stacked sensors that separate colors by depth within one pixel.
